steps.title: Prove the hazard: a stall outlives the lease
steps.instructions:
Now break it on purpose, the exact way production breaks it. A holder checks its lock with GET, stalls, and its DEL lands after the world moved on:

```go
    // --- The hazard: a stall outlives the lease, and a naive DEL
    // destroys the winner's lock.
    if err := rdb.Del(ctx, lockKey).Err(); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    tokenA3, _ := acquireLock(ctx, rdb, lockKey)
    fmt.Printf("holder A acquired; its work stalls %s\n", stall)

    stored, err := rdb.Get(ctx, lockKey).Result() // GET: still mine?
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println("A's GET says the lock is mine:", stored == tokenA3)

    time.Sleep(stall) // the 2s lease expires in here

    _, wonB := acquireLock(ctx, rdb, lockKey)
    fmt.Println("holder B acquired after the lapse:", wonB)

    rdb.Del(ctx, lockKey) // A's DEL lands late — no check, no token: B's lock
    report(ctx, rdb, "  after A's naive DEL")

    tokenC, wonC := acquireLock(ctx, rdb, lockKey)
    fmt.Println("holder C walks in while B still works:", wonC)
    ok, _ = safeUnlock(ctx, rdb, lockKey, tokenC)
    fmt.Println("C released with its own token:", ok)
    fmt.Println()
```

Read it as a timeline. A GETs its own token — mine — then stalls; the 2-second lease lapses inside that sleep, silently (MONITOR shows no del when a key expires — it simply stops existing); B's SetNX now wins against an absent key; and finally A's DEL — the second half of its GET-then-DEL, written long before the world changed — lands on a lock it no longer owns. B did nothing wrong and holds the only valid claim, yet its protection is gone: the proof is C walking straight in while B still believes it is working under the lock. Note what the demo says about the checked version too — the GET did fire, and did say mine; the hole is that the check and the delete are two round-trips, and the stall can sit between them exactly where this sleep sits. Watch the takeover from a second terminal while the program runs:

```
redis-cli MONITOR
```

Acquires arrive as `set job:nightly-report:lock <token> ex 2 nx` — B's succeeds only because the server has no key left to refuse — and A's naive unlock is the one bare `del`. Script releases arrive as `evalsha`, with the script's own `get`/`del` shown underneath as `[0 lua]` lines.

holder A acquired; its work stalls 2.5s
A's GET says the lock is mine: true

steps.title: Run it whole, then name the limitation: fencing
steps.instructions:
Run the finished program end to end — it takes about five seconds, two deliberate stalls included:

```

```

Every line now has a name. Act one is the contract: acquire is exclusive, release is token-checked, re-acquire proves release. Act two is the hazard: the lease lapsed, the naive DEL destroyed a lock the deleter did not own, and a third holder walked in. Act three is the same timeline with the script in the unlock path: the stale token refused, B's lease still running, B's own release honored. Then name the limitation, because the demo has been showing it all along: everything safeUnlock protected was the lock key, not the resource. Nothing revokes a stalled holder's in-memory belief that it holds the lock — A can go on writing the nightly report after B owns the lock, and compare-and-del stops the wrong DEL, never the wrong write. The standard next step is a fencing token: each acquire also returns a number that increases every time (one INCR on a separate key mints them), every write to the resource must carry its number, and the resource rejects any write whose number is below the highest it has accepted. That turns who-holds-the-lock from an assumption the resource must trust into a check the resource enforces — which is also its price: the storage has to cooperate, and most offer no such check. And this remains a single-instance lock: it lives and dies with one Redis server, and a failover can lose a lock that was already acked because replication is asynchronous — the multi-node Redlock debate exists precisely here. For many jobs an advisory token-and-lease lock of exactly this shape is the right budget; the discipline is knowing which kind your job is.

title: Rate limiting: fixed and sliding windows
prerequisites: Everyday Go fluency: modules and go.mod, error handling with the errors package (errors.Is, wrapping), and context.Context as the first argument of every blocking call.

The structures tour's TTL idiom — branch on ttl < 0 and read -1ns/-2ns as answers, not errors — is assumed here, because the fixed window's safety net is built from exactly that branch; the sliding window arrives as one short Lua script you read line by line, no Lua background needed.
summary: Go client practice — not exam prep: the Redis Associate Developer certification is Java-specific, and intermediate here means comfortable reading Go that handles errors and contexts, not a Redis veteran. Build two rate limiters over the same budget — five hits per ten seconds — on go-redis v9: a fixed window from Incr plus a first-hit Expire, including the non-atomicity gap between the two calls, where a crash leaves the window key TTL-less and that client permanently locked out, healed by the ttl < 0 re-arm guard; then a sliding window whose entire bookkeeping — zadd, zremrangebyscore, zcard, expire — lives inside one Lua script, leaving the Go surface a single script.Run. Over-limit rejection and window reset are proved from redis-cli, by reading GET, ZCARD, and TTL off the window keys. The linked performance lesson is the related core reading: its single-threaded event loop is why one atomic script beats four interleaved round trips, and its SLOWLOG-and-MONITOR toolbox is how the cost question this lab raises — one counter versus a sorted-set member per hit — becomes measurement.

No client-side recipe closes that hole completely, which is why the ttl < 0 guard is worth keeping under either version — it is the layer that self-heals whatever slips through.

steps.title: Sliding window: one Lua script owns the bookkeeping
steps.instructions:
A sliding window with the same budget needs a different shape: not a counter but a sorted set of hits — score = when, member = which hit — where 'in window' means 'score within the last ten seconds'. Four commands do the bookkeeping: trim expired members (zremrangebyscore), count the survivors (zcard), maybe record this hit (zadd), and keep the key's lease fresh (expire). Issued from Go as four round trips they interleave badly — two clients can trim, count, and add against each other's unfinished state. So the bookkeeping lives where interleaving cannot reach: one Lua script, which the server runs atomically:

```go
// slidingScript performs the entire sliding-window bookkeeping in one atomic
// execution: trim expired hits, count the survivors, admit or reject, and
// keep the key's lease fresh. The Go side never touches the zset itself.
var slidingScript = redis.NewScript(`
local now    = tonumber(ARGV[1])  -- hit time, ms since epoch
local window = tonumber(ARGV[2])  -- window length, ms
local limit  = tonumber(ARGV[3])

redis.call('zremrangebyscore', KEYS[1], '-inf', now - window)
if redis.call('zcard', KEYS[1]) < limit then
	redis.call('zadd', KEYS[1], now, ARGV[4])  -- ARGV[4]: unique member per hit
	redis.call('expire', KEYS[1], math.ceil(window / 1000))
	return 1
end
return 0
`)

func slidingWindowAllow(ctx context.Context, rdb *redis.Client, key string) (bool, error) {
    allowed, err := slidingScript.Run(ctx, rdb, []string{key},
        time.Now().UnixMilli(), // ARGV[1] — now
        window.Milliseconds(),  // ARGV[2] — window length
        limit,                  // ARGV[3]
        time.Now().UnixNano(),  // ARGV[4] — unique member per hit
    ).Int()
    if err != nil {
        return false, err
    }
    return allowed == 1, nil
}
```

redis.NewScript caches the source client-side and Run executes EVALSHA with an automatic EVAL fallback — the same pair the distributed lock's compare-and-del used. KEYS[1] is the zset key; the four ARGV values are now, the window, the limit, and a unique member for this hit. Scores stay in milliseconds — small enough that float64 holds them exactly, which scores beyond 2^53 would not be — while the member carries the uniqueness as a nanosecond string, so two hits in the same millisecond still get distinct entries. And because the trim, the count, the zadd, and the expire share one atomic execution, this key can never be caught TTL-less: the fixed window's orphan is structurally impossible here.

Then give the sliding window the same seven-hit trial in `main`:

```go
    fmt.Println("--- sliding window ---")
    for i := 1; i <= limit+2; i++ {
        allowed, err := slidingWindowAllow(ctx, rdb, slidingKey)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        fmt.Printf("hit %d: %s\n", i, verdict(allowed))
    }
```

Your fixed block may continue a previous window — after step 4's orphan rerun the count stands at 14 — wait out its TTL and rerun for the clean replay. The sliding block rejects hits 6 and 7 exactly as the fixed window did: same budget. The difference is inside the key, and the next step reads it.

steps.solution: Why a nanosecond string as the member rather than the millisecond score itself? zadd members must be unique — two members with the same bytes collapse into one entry, and a same-millisecond pair of hits would count as one, quietly loosening the limit. Unique members cost nothing: the score orders the window, the member only has to differ.

steps.title: Read both windows from redis-cli, and weigh the trade
steps.instructions:
Give both windows a clean run: wait out any open TTL — GET on a window key answering nil tells you it is closed — then run the program once and read both keys:

```
GET ratelimit:fixed:alice
ZRANGE ratelimit:sliding:alice 0 -1 WITHSCORES
ZCARD ratelimit:sliding:alice
TTL ratelimit:fixed:alice
TTL ratelimit:sliding:alice
```

The fixed key holds one string, 7 — every hit counted, rejects included. The sliding key is a zset of exactly five members, each a nanosecond string scored with its millisecond timestamp: the seven-hit trial recorded five, because the two rejected hits never entered the zset. Both TTLs answer positive countdowns — neither window can outlive its lease.

Now wait out the window once more and read again:

```
GET ratelimit:fixed:alice
ZRANGE ratelimit:sliding:alice 0 -1
TTL ratelimit:fixed:alice
```

Both keys are gone on their own — GET answers nil, ZRANGE answers an empty array, TTL answers -2, the missing sentinel your Go `ttl < 0` branch exists for — and a rerun replays both budgets from their first hit.

The trade, named: the fixed window costs one string and two round trips per hit, and pays in boundary bursts — a client can spend all five hits in the last instant of one window and five more in the first instant of the next, double the budget across the seam. The sliding window admits exactly five in any ten seconds, never records a rejection, and pays for it: a zset member per admitted hit and a script evaluation per hit of any kind. Which budget a service can afford is a measurement question — the linked performance lesson's SLOWLOG and MONITOR are where that question gets answered.

You can harden the fixed window with the ttl < 0 guard — read TTL on every hit and re-arm on a raw -1ns/-2ns sentinel — and say which races remain: a double-Expire that harmlessly nudges the boundary, and healing on the next hit rather than prevention at the crash; SetNX's atomic first hit prevents the orphan but keeps a smaller race of its own.

You can put an entire sliding window's bookkeeping — zremrangebyscore, zcard, zadd, expire — inside one Lua script run via redis.NewScript and script.Run, so the Go surface is a single atomic call and the window key can never be caught TTL-less.

You can prove both limiters' behavior from redis-cli — GET answering 7 while ZCARD answers 5 for the same seven hits, positive TTLs on both window keys, nil and -2 after the wait — and name the trade: boundary bursts with O(1) storage versus exact admission with a member per hit.

title: Streams consumer groups in Go
prerequisites: Everyday Go fluency: modules and go.mod, error handling with the errors package (errors.Is, wrapping), and context.Context as the first argument of every blocking call.

No goroutines required: worker-a and worker-b are just two names the server tracks, played in sequence from one main. What the lab does need is patience for deliberate waits — a three-second sleep ages one pending entry past MinIdle so the reclaim has something to reclaim, and a two-second block proves a drained pipeline answers instead of hangs.
summary: Go client practice — not exam prep: the Redis Associate Developer certification is Java-specific, and advanced here means the earlier Go labs' idioms — errors.Is, ctx-first calls, reading a struct literal that mirrors its redis-cli command word for word — are reflexes now. Run one order pipeline through the full consumer-group lifecycle on go-redis v9: XAdd thirty orders into a stream capped by MaxLen (an int64 that trims as each entry lands) and collect the server-assigned <ms>-<seq> IDs; XGroupCreate at "0" rather than "$"; then XReadGroup with the Streams pair []string{stream, ">"}, Count 10, and Block held to a finite 2s — Block: 0 compiles to an indefinite BLOCK 0, a shape reserved for consumer loops that own a cancelable context. worker-a acks nine entries in one variadic XAck and crashes before the tenth, and the lab watches the delivery become a pending entry: XPending's summary, then XPendingExt's ID, consumer, idle, and retry count, the idle time growing past MinIdle while nobody is home. worker-b reclaims with XAutoClaim — Redis ≥6.2 is a hard floor here, because that is where XAUTOCLAIM landed — taking the full message back plus the next-scan cursor, with the retry count bumped to 2 before the ack empties the PEL. That is at-least-once delivery, and the lab names its price: duplicates are part of the contract, handlers must be idempotent, and a blocked-empty read answers errors.Is(err, redis.Nil) — the structures tour's miss sentinel with a streams meaning. The linked data-structures lesson is the related core reading: its streams section defines the machinery this lab drives — last-delivered IDs, per-consumer pending-entries lists, ">" as never-delivered-to-this-group — and its reply shapes are exactly what these Go calls return.

steps.instructions:
You need Go 1.24 or newer, a local `redis-server` ≥6.2 — the pack's floor, and this lab's own requirement: XAUTOCLAIM, the reclaim command at the heart of step 5, landed in Redis 6.2 — and redis-cli for verifying from outside the program. Scaffold a fresh module so this lab's pipeline owns its namespace:

```
mkdir go-streams && cd go-streams
go mod init streams
go get github.com/redis/go-redis/v9@v9.22.0
```

go.mod picks up `go 1.24` and `github.com/redis/go-redis/v9 v9.22.0`; anything ≥9.16 works for this pack, and 9.15.0 — the broken, retracted release the earlier Go labs warned about — is still a version never to pin. Create `main.go` with the client and the pipeline's eight constants:

```go
package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "time"

    "github.com/redis/go-redis/v9"
)

const (
    stream    = "orders:stream"
    group     = "order-workers"
    workerA   = "worker-a"
    workerB   = "worker-b"
    maxLen    = int64(10)       // MAXLEN: the stream never holds more than this
    readCount = int64(10)       // COUNT: max entries per XReadGroup
    block     = 2 * time.Second // finite BLOCK: the walkthrough must never hang
    minIdle   = 2 * time.Second // XAUTOCLAIM's MINIDLE: claim only entries idle this long
)

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()

    rdb := redis.NewClient(&redis.Options{Addr: "localhost:6379"})
    defer rdb.Close()

    if err := rdb.Ping(ctx).Err(); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println("connected: one stream, one group, two consumers")

    // Fresh replay every run: DEL takes the stream, its group, and every
    // pending-entries list on it with it. All of that is server state.
    if err := rdb.Del(ctx, stream).Err(); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}
```

`go run .` prints `connected: one stream, one group, two consumers`. The constants encode the lab's whole design: a stream capped at ten so the trim is visible after a thirty-order burst, a read cap of ten so worker-a drains the backlog in one call, and two durations measured in seconds so the full story fits in one run. The Del at the top is the reset button — unlike the rate limiter's counters, everything this lab creates (entries, the group, per-consumer pending lists) is attached to the one key, so one Del is a clean slate.

steps.hint: If the claim comes back empty and printPEL still says worker-a, the entry's idle never reached MinIdle — the sleep is only 3s against a 2s MinIdle, and a debugger breakpoint can eat the margin. Bump the sleep or lower minIdle.
steps.solution: Why gate on MinIdle at all — why not let worker-b take every pending entry it can see? Because pending does not mean dead: a worker grinding through a ten-second transcode holds a legitimately pending entry the whole time. MinIdle is the difference between failover and theft, and it is why production values are minutes, not the two seconds this demo can afford. The cursor exists for the same reason: a real PEL can hold thousands of entries and one call scans at most Count of them, so you page with next until it answers 0-0.

steps.title: Read into silence, then verify the pipeline from redis-cli
steps.expectedOutput:
after 2.1s the blocked read answered redis.Nil: nothing new, no error, no hang
Then from redis-cli: XLEN answers 10; XPENDING answers 0; XINFO GROUPS reports name order-workers, consumers 2, pending 0, last-delivered-id at the newest entry; XINFO CONSUMERS lists worker-a and worker-b, both pending 0; XRANGE lists order-21 (user user-3, total 220) then order-22 (user user-1, total 221), fields exactly as produced.
steps.hint: If the final read returns entries instead of silence, they landed after worker-a's read — the ">" ID only skips entries the group has already delivered, so anything XAdded mid-run gets delivered normally. Produce, then group up, then read: order matters.

outcomes: A runnable Go producer over a capped stream: XAdd with Values as a map[string]interface{} and MaxLen as an int64 that trims as each entry lands — exact trimming holds XLEN at 10 through a thirty-order burst, Approx: true trims in whole nodes and leaves a stream this small untouched — and every call returns the server-assigned <ms>-<seq> ID that ack and reclaim both key off.

You can create a group at the right position — XGroupCreate at "0" replays history, "$" waits for new entries — and read with XReadGroup's Streams pair []string{stream, ">"}, Count, and a finite Block, able to state all three Block settings: positive waits that long, 0 compiles to an indefinite BLOCK 0 for cancelable consumer loops only, negative disables BLOCK.

You can prove at-least-once delivery end to end: skip an ack and the entry pends — XPending's summary, then XPendingExt's ID, consumer, idle, and retry count, idle growing past MinIdle while nobody is home — XAutoClaim from a second consumer moves the entry and bumps its retry count to 2, and the ack drops the pending count to 0.

You can name the operational costs: duplicates are part of the contract, so handlers are idempotent and the retry count is the meter; a blocked-empty read answers errors.Is(err, redis.Nil), the structures tour's miss sentinel with a streams meaning; and the whole pipeline — entries, group, PEL, consumers — is server state that one DEL tears down.
checks: Flip Approx to true in produce, rerun, and read XLEN orders:stream: it answers 30, not 10 — the ~ trim works in whole radix-tree nodes and a 30-entry stream is smaller than one. Set Approx back to false, confirm XLEN returns to 10, and say which setting a production producer uses and why a demo cannot.

Delete worker-b's ack loop from reclaimStuck (keep the claim print above it), rerun, and confirm "XPENDING after the ack" reads 1 — then from redis-cli, XPENDING orders:stream order-workers - + 10 answers the entry with consumer worker-b and a delivery count of 2: XAutoClaim moved it, only the ack retires it. Restore the loop, rerun, confirm 0.

Change only the XAutoClaim call's MinIdle to 30 * time.Second, rerun, and confirm the claim comes back empty while printPEL still names worker-a with retries=1 — then say in one sentence what MinIdle protects a live-but-slow worker from.

Point at both XReadGroup calls in the finished program and answer without running: what would each do with Block: 0, and where does that setting belong? Then set block to -time.Second in the const block and rerun: the final read answers redis.Nil instantly instead of after two seconds — a negative Block disables BLOCK entirely.
